items.text: You weren't spending energy you had. You were borrowing it. Masking debt is real — and burnout is just the moment the interest comes due.
items.rationale: Punchy encapsulation of the masking-debt frame. The borrowing metaphor does the conceptual work without over-explaining. Lands as recognition, not lecture. Quote-card ready.

items.text: Burnout isn't a personal failure. It's the predictable outcome when the cost of masking outpaces what rest and safety put back. The math always catches up.
items.rationale: Extends the masking-debt angle without repeating it — shifts from metaphor to structural logic. Removes blame explicitly while staying dry and unsentimental.

items.text: We keep asking why autistic people struggle at work. Better question: why are workplaces designed so only some brains have to pay a second, invisible salary to belong?
items.rationale: Shifts the problem from individual to structural with a concrete image ('second salary'). Meets real frustration without outrage-bait because it stays analytical. Directly sourced from Feb 2026 piece.

items.text: Wanting to do the thing. Knowing you want to do the thing. Still hitting an invisible wall the moment it starts to feel like a demand. That's not willpower failure. That's a threat response.
items.rationale: Names the specific PDA experience — wanting the goal but blocked by the demand structure — with precision most content never achieves. 'Threat response' is the key reframe from the sourced clinical framing.
items.sensitivity_flag: Definitive 'That's a threat response' reads as near-clinical. Defensible given the therapy source explicitly uses this frame, but consider softening to 'can be a threat response' if the platform applies strict health-content review.

items.text: When the accommodation that finally worked gets quietly removed — is that just a policy change? What did remote work actually give you that the office couldn't?
items.rationale: Embeds the reframe ('accommodation that finally worked') inside the question itself so the framing lands even if readers don't engage. Opens genuine testimony threads without manufacturing outrage.

items.text: Biographical illumination: when a late diagnosis doesn't change who you were — it finally explains it. Every chapter you thought you'd misread suddenly makes sense.
items.rationale: Introduces a named concept from peer-reviewed research that the community doesn't widely have language for yet. High originality, strong recognition potential for late-diagnosed readers. The term does the work; no over-explanation needed.

items.text: Autistic burnout and depression overlap — but they're not the same. Burnout often lifts when demands drop. Depression doesn't work that way. Treating one as the other can make both worse.
items.rationale: Directly useful community health literacy: gives people a clean differentiator to inform self-advocacy and conversations with clinicians. Names concrete harm without blame. Stays at pattern level, not personal instruction.
items.sensitivity_flag: Draws a functional distinction between conditions — acceptable as community-level literacy, not treatment advice, but worth a second look if the platform has strict health-content policies. Both-can-be-true nuance is implied but could be made explicit.

items.text: If you're AuDHD and feel like you fall between both communities rather than fully in either — that's not you failing to fit the labels. It's the labels failing to fit you.
items.rationale: Directly addresses the under-named experience of partial belonging in both ADHD and autism spaces. Challenges siloed framing without being combative. High recognition potential; backed by 2026 SAGE research.

items.text: Low demand parenting doesn't mean no demands. It means asking: is this demand load-bearing, or is it just habit? One is worth the effort. One isn't.
items.rationale: Addresses the most common and damaging misread of the approach directly. Validates the labour of precision parenting without being defensive. Clean enough to screenshot and share with a skeptical family member.

items.text: Stimming isn't dysregulation. For many autistic people, it's how the nervous system gets accurate information about itself.
items.rationale: Leads with the reframe, lets the interoception mechanism do the work without naming jargon. Short, quote-card ready. Shifts the stimming narrative from something to manage to something that serves a function.
items.sensitivity_flag: Source is a bioRxiv preprint — not yet peer-reviewed. The stimming-heartbeat-detection finding is specific and quotable but should be framed as 'research suggests' or caveated as preliminary before publishing.

items.text: Your brain needs to know someone is present — not necessarily who. Research is catching up to what the community already knew: AI body doubles can work just as well.
items.rationale: Community-discovery-before-science narrative is reliably engaging. Immediately actionable takeaway (AI tools and virtual co-working count). 'Can work just as well' is appropriately hedged rather than absolute.
items.sensitivity_flag: Equivalence claim is based on a single ACM study with limited scope. 'Can work just as well' is defensible but verify sample size and conditions before publishing — avoid upgrading to 'works just as well' in any caption copy.

items.text: For many neurodivergent workers, remote work wasn't a perk. It was the first workplace accommodation that actually worked. RTO doesn't just change where people sit.
items.rationale: Reframes the RTO debate from productivity to access without producing outrage. The last sentence lands as understatement — which hits harder than a more explicit conclusion. Shareable by community members and HR readers alike.
